A price target is a forecast of the future price of an asset. Price targets are provided by CPM group, an independent research advisory firm.

Demand for jewellery has been known to be very sensitive to the price of the metal, and the forecast price plays the most important role in determining the level of jewellery demand. Expectations of price volatility and discretionary income levels also are forecasted and given consideration in projecting the level of precious metals demand from the jewellery sector. This also includes advertising spending on specific metals’ jewellery and expected fashion trends.

Investment demand is the most powerful fundamental in terms of its influence on precious metals prices. Hence, it is considered as the \'prime mover\' or most important factor affecting precious metals prices.

CPM Group incorporates new and expansion mining projects into its forward supply curve based on the assessed economic viability of individual projects.

Mine supply from producing mines is based on the mine’s reserves and resources as well as the company’s forecasts, the projected mine life at existing and projected projects, and the company’s annual production profile.
Supply from existing mines as well as new and expansion projects is handicapped to reflect variations in precious metals prices and unexpected disruptions like natural calamities or labour strikes.

Macroeconomic metrics such as interest rates, inflation, currency volatility, the general economic health of the global economy, and potential threats to economic growth have varying impacts on precious metals. Investors typically purchase gold and silver as a hedge against inflation and currency market fluctuations. The collective outcome of each of these factors is used as a gauge of the forecast level of investment demand for each of the precious metals in any given year.
CPM uses a range of methodologies to analyse and forecast price targets for precious metals

Projections for secondary supply or scrap supply are based on estimates provided by refiners and consultants based in the large secondary recovery markets, like the United States, China, Europe, Dubai, and India. The precious metals prices, government regulations, life of product (in the case of electronics, and dental materials, and autocatalysts), and the level of thrifting (per unit reduction in the use of precious metals) are all factors that are used to determine the level of future secondary supply.

When will I be charged interest?

This is the time between the end of your billing cycle and your statement\'s due date. During this time, we don’t charge interest on your purchases, as long as you pay your full balance by the due date. The number of days in the grace period may vary, especially if the due date falls on a weekend or holiday. We’ll include any purchases you make during this period in the next billing cycle, so they’ll show on your next statement.

We’ll charge daily interest on the overdue amount from your last statement. We’ll charge this from the due date, until you make the minimum monthly repayment. The rate of interest we’ll charge is shown on your last PDF statement.

We won’t charge any interest if you pay your statement balance in full by the statement due date. If you miss the statement due date, you can reduce the amount of interest by paying the balance as soon as possible.

How can I increase my limit?

Unlike your statement which is issued monthly, your credit limit does not have a fixed renewal cycle. If you’ve used up a part of your limit, simply make a payment at any time to increase the amount of available funds from your limit.

When does my credit limit renew?

We will always let you know when you’ve used up most of your limit, but if you do go over it, you won’t be able to use your credit card until you make a payment to bring your balance back within your agreed limit. We do not currently charge any additional fees for exceeding your limit.

If you pay your statement balance in full by the due date, you will receive a grace period lasting up to two calendar months, during which interest is not applied to card purchases. Cash withdrawals and other types of transactions do not have a grace period and accrue interest from the day your transaction is completed.

Interest is calculated using daily average balance method and accrues each day. For purchases, interest will be applied to your balance if the full statement balance hasn’t been repaid in full by the payment due date. For cash withdrawals and transfers, interest is accrued and payable from the day of your transaction completion till it’s repaid in full.

By paying your statement balance in full by the payment due each month you will not be charged interest for card purchases. If you carry over a balance or make a transaction which isn’t considered a card purchase, you can reduce the amount of interest charged by paying the balance as soon as possible.

Revolut Digital Assets Europe Ltd (Revolut) provides two channels for executing cryptocurrency transactions: the Revolut App and Revolut X (mobile and web). Each operates under a distinct execution framework.

Revolut App — Over-The-Counter execution model: Revolut acts as counterparty to all trades. Pricing is proprietary, derived from internal algorithms referencing external data, but not directly linked to third-party order books.

Revolut X — Operation of a Trading Platform execution model: Revolut operates a trading platform where user orders are matched via a central limit order book. Pricing is determined by market supply and demand within the order book.

Both platforms support spot instruments only, with immediate settlement. Revolut X also offers advanced order types and API connectivity.

Revolut App

  • Trades executed at fixed quoted price (guaranteed once accepted).
  • Revolut acts as principal; pricing may differ from external market rates.
  • Maximum order sizes apply.
  • Revolut may pause pricing or reject orders during extreme volatility.
  • Provides certainty and ease of use, but no access to live market pricing or order types.

Revolut X

  • Trades matched with other users on a live order book.
  • Market orders execute at best available price (not guaranteed).
  • Limit orders remain open until filled or cancelled.
  • Slippage and partial fills are possible, especially in volatile or illiquid markets.
  • Minimum order size applies.
  • Designed for experienced users; offers advanced tools but with higher execution risk.

• Trades are executed at a fixed price quoted in-app at the time of confirmation (price is guaranteed once accepted).
  • Pricing is provided by Revolut acting as principal, and may differ from market exchange rates.
  • Maximum order sizes apply to manage volatility.
  • During extreme market conditions, Revolut may pause pricing or reject orders.
  • Offers price certainty and ease of use, but does not provide access to full market pricing or order types.

• Trades are matched with other users on a live order book. Market orders execute at the best available price- this may differ from the last quoted price (no guaranteed execution price).
  • Limit orders remain open until filled or cancelled.
  • Slippage may occur, especially during market volatility.
  • Large orders may be partially filled or rejected if liquidity is low.
  • Minimum order size applies.
  • Designed for experienced users; offers advanced features (e.g. API trading) but carries higher execution risk.

Revolut App — Principal: Revolut is the counterparty to all trades. Customers transact directly with Revolut, not with other market participants. Prices quoted at confirmation are binding once accepted. This model provides price certainty and a simplified interface but does not give access to market order books. Revolut may manage spreads internally and suspend pricing during volatility.

Revolut X — Neutral Facilitator: Revolut provides infrastructure for peer-to-peer execution. Orders are matched on a central order book by time and price priority. Revolut does not act as counterparty or take proprietary positions. Users assume execution risk (e.g. slippage, partial fills, unfilled orders). The platform is designed for more sophisticated users and includes advanced tools, analytics, and APIs.
Revolut offers two ways to trade crypto: Revolut app and Revolut X, with different models and pricing. See comparison below. Services are provided by Revolut Digital Assets Europe Ltd
What’s the difference between Crypto in Revolut App and Revolut X?

Revolut charges fees for executing crypto trades, with structures differing between the Revolut App and Revolut X.

On the Revolut App, retail users pay either a minimum fee or a tiered percentage fee, whichever is higher. The percentage depends on the subscription plan and total crypto trading volume over a rolling 30-day period. Minimum fees vary by plan and trade size, and the tiered rate decreases as trading volume increases. Some transactions, such as stablecoin-to-fiat trades, are excluded from the volume calculation. In all cases, the app shows the exchange rate, fee, and total cost before confirmation.

On Revolut X, retail users are charged according to a maker-taker model. Maker orders (adding liquidity) incur a 0.00% fee, while Taker orders (removing liquidity) incur a 0.09% fee. No minimum fees apply.

Detailed fee schedules and terms are available on our Revolut X Fees Page and Retail Fees Pages

DeFi tokens, such as AAVE, are associated with decentralised financial applications, but they come with specific risks.

• Smart contract risk: Vulnerabilities in smart contracts may be exploited and lead to significant losses.
• Scam risk: Bad actors may launch tokens with no real intention of developing the project, resulting in the exploitation of investors and complete loss of funds.
• Data risk: Reliance by some protocols on external data sources, which may be vulnerable to attack, could result in disruption and devaluation.
• Protocol complexity: Understanding the intricate nature of DeFi protocols can be challenging, take time to educate yourself.

Meme coins, like DOGE, derive their value from online trends, resulting in distinct risks.

• Volatility risk: Rapid and unpredictable price fluctuations are common, with value reliant on community interest, social media trends and speculation.
• Market abuse: High vulnerability to market manipulation schemes, such as pump-and-dump, where value can crash instantly.
• Lack of transparency: Limited information about development teams and financials mean traditional market value assessments cannot be done.
• Emotional investing: Emotional reactions can lead to impulsive decisions and amplify your losses.

\"Stablecoins\", such as USDT and USDC, are cryptoassets whose value is linked to reserve assets like the US Dollar (or other cryptoassets), and which seek to maintain stability through various methods, each carrying distinct risks.

• Collateral risk: Fluctuations in the value of collateral may impact price stability.
• Redemption risk: Redemption processes might not work efficiently during market volatility or operational incidents.
• FX risk: Depending upon your base currency, exposure to exchange rate fluctuations (from/to USD) may impact the value of your investment.
• Counterparty risk: The management of collateral maintenance depends upon third-parties, over which you have no control.

Staking cryptoassets, like DOT or ETH, locks your assets for network security and rewards, but come with risks:

• Slashing: A potential penalty (loss of assets) due to validator non-compliance.
• Liquidity risk: some tokens involve a lock-up period, meaning you will have to wait before you are able to sell tokens.
• APY not guaranteed: Reward rates are subject to change and are not guaranteed.
• Consensus risks: Changes to how a protocol is validated (how ‘consensus’ is reached), can introduce new, unexpected vulnerabilities.

Wrapped cryptoassets, like wAXL, represent cryptoassets native to another blockchain, and are typically used to facilitate interaction between different blockchains, but they carry risks.

• Collateral risk: Failures to adequately collateralise the underlying tokens could destabilise the wrapped value.
• Custodial risk: Underlying assets may be held with third-party custodians, who could be exposed to an insolvency or cyber crime event. This can impact the value of the wrapped tokens.
• Smart contract risk: Vulnerabilities in smart contracts could be exposed and lead to fund losses.
• Bridging risk: Technical issues in integration layers between protocols (‘Bridges’) can disrupt token movement or redemption.
• Price divergence: A liquidity crisis, or other market issue, might cause price disparities between the wrapped token and its underlying asset.

Exchange Traded Commodities (ETCs) are debt securities that provide exposure to the price of a specific commodity, a basket of commodities or a commodity index such as gold, silver, oil, or natural gas.
Crypto Exchange Traded Notes (“cETNs”) are debt securities that provide exposure to an underlying crypto-asset or index (e.g. Bitcoin or Ethereum)
Don’t invest unless you’re prepared to lose all the money you invest. This is a high-risk investment and you are unlikely to be protected if something goes wrong.
For further information about cryptoassets, visit the FCA’s website

• Putting all your money into a single type of investment is risky. Spreading your money across different investments makes you less dependent on any one to do well.\n• A good rule of thumb is not to invest more than 10% of your money in high-risk investments.
Don’t put all your eggs in one basket

Please note that this is a high-risk investment. How would you feel if you lost the money you’re about to invest? Don’t invest unless you’re prepared to lose all the money you invest. This is a high-risk investment and you should not expect to be protected if something goes wrong. Take 2 mins to learn more.

• The performance of most cryptoassets can be highly volatile, with their value dropping as quickly as it can rise. You should be prepared to lose all the money you invest in cryptoasset exchange traded notes.\n• The cryptoasset market is largely unregulated. There is a risk of losing money due to risks such as cyber-attacks, financial crime and firm failure.
You could lose all the money you invest

• The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) doesn’t protect this type of investment because it’s not a type of investment that the FSCS can protect.\n• Protection from the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) does not cover poor investment performance. If you have a complaint against an FCA-regulated firm, FOS may be able to consider it.
You should not expect to be protected if something goes wrong

Delisting is the removal of a listed security from a stock exchange. The delisting of a security can be voluntary or involuntary and usually results when a company ceases operations, declares bankruptcy, does not meet listing requirements, or seeks to become private.

A listed company is a public company. It has issued shares of its stock through an exchange, with each share representing a piece of ownership of the company. Those shares can then be bought and sold by investors, rising or falling in value according to demand.
A stock that has recently gone public and has been listed on an exchange for purchase.

Trade resumption is the commencement of trading activities after they have been shut down for a period of time, halted or the resumption of trade between nations. Trade resumption occurs after events, such as a pending news announcement, an order imbalance, or other regulatory reasons, cause a trading halt.

A situation in which trading on a security is stopped as a result of a trading halt or similar event. Trading halts are typically enacted in anticipation of a news announcement, to correct an order imbalance, as a result of a technical glitch, volatility, or due to regulatory concerns. When a trading halt is in effect, open orders will be in Pending state until trading is resumed.

P/E ratio is the stock\'s current price divided by its earnings per share. The higher the ratio the more you are paying for the earnings of a stock

PEG ratio is the Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio divided by expected earnings growth, used to assess whether a stock may be over- or undervalued relative to its growth. The higher the ratio the more you\'re paying for the earnings of a stock in relation to its growth

P/S ratio is a stock\'s price divided by its annual revenue per share. P/S ratio may be useful for valuing companies that are not yet profitable

P/B ratio is a stock\'s market price divided by the company\'s book value per share, indicating how much investors pay relative to the company\'s net worth. A lower ratio indicates that the price is closer to the company\'s net worth

P/FCF ratio is a stock\'s price divided by the company\'s free cash flow per share, indicating how much investors pay for 1 unit of currency of cash generated after operating costs. A lower ratio indicates that the price is closer to the company\'s available cash after operating costs

Money market funds are a type of mutual fund that invests in high quality, short-term debt securities. Money market funds are considered low risk investments. Money market funds do not rely on external support to guarantee their liquidity or the stability of the Net Asset Value per share.
Past performance is no guarantee of future returns. The return generated by your investment will be re-invested monthly on your behalf.

Net Annual Percentage Yield represents the final return you get from your money. It changes daily and is calculated from the Gross return rate (the overall fund return, excluding service fees and taxes). This rate is not guaranteed and the value of your investment can go up as well as down. The return generated by your investment will be re-invested on your behalf at the beginning of the next month if you don’t withdraw it. The APY shown is today\'s applicable rate.

Set a target value for the currency of your choice and we’ll automatically exchange it once the price hits your target. We’ll use the best available rate, but just like us the exchange rate never settles! This means the rate could be slightly different from your target value, when the auto-exchange takes place.

If your account is blocked for any reason, we wouldn’t be able to carry out any auto-exchanges. Once your account is back in action your auto-exchange will start working again and you won’t need to reschedule anything.
You are limited to a maximum of €15,000 per single cryptocurrency exchange and 30 exchanges per day. Once you\'ve hit your limit, you won\'t be able to make any more exchanges until the next day.
You are limited to a maximum of $15,000 per single cryptocurrency exchange and 30 exchanges per day. Once you\'ve hit your limit, you won\'t be able to make any more exchanges until the next day.
We limit the amount of auto-exchanges to 30 per day, so any exchanges that are triggered after you’ve hit your limit would fail. If you wait until the next day, you’ll be able to schedule another.

If you don’t have enough money in your account when the auto-exchange is due, your exchange will fail. If this happens, all you would need to do is top-up your account and schedule another auto-exchange.

If the market is particularly volatile, your target value might have shifted in the brief window between the target value being hit, and the auto-exchange being performed. If the rate moves more than 0.75% either side of your target value for fiat currencies, or 5% for cryptocurrencies, we won’t carry out your auto-exchange. Once your target value hits again, we’ll re-attempt the auto-exchange.

Understanding the source of our users' money is important for a number of reasons:
∙ To verify that the transactions made were actually completed by you
∙ To protect all of our users and their money from fraud, or from being linked to illegal activities
∙ To comply with the relevant laws and regulations that allow us to operate as a financial institution

This indicates whether the issuer can redeem the bond before its maturity date. If ‘yes’, the issuer can choose to exercise the call option on the bond. If ‘no’, the bond can only be redeemed at maturity.
This is the earliest date the issuer will repay the bond if they choose to exercise the call option.
This is the amount the issuer will pay to bondholders if they choose to exercise the call option. It\'s usually more than the face value of the bond.
The currency in which the bond is traded.
The amount the issuer pays back to the bondholder for each lot of bond they own once it reaches maturity.
An International Securities Identification Number (ISIN) is an alphanumeric code which uniquely identifies a specific security or other financial instrument.
The date on which the bond begins to accrue interest.
The initial price at which the bond issuer originally sells the bond.
The date on which the bond reaches the end of its life and the original investment amount is repaid to the holder.
The total value of this bond available in the market in the base currency of the bond.
The frequency at which an issuer pays the coupon to the holder. Bonds typically pay interest monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, or annually.

The coupon type defines how the coupon is calculated throughout the life of the bond. A fixed-rate coupon maintains the same rate until maturity, while a floating-rate bond has a changing rate tied to a benchmark. A zero-coupon bond does not pay any coupons.
The annual interest rate paid on a bond, expressed as a percentage of the face value.
The date on which the next coupon will be paid to the bondholder.

Credit quality is a measure of the issuer’s likelihood to meet its debt obligations.
\'D\' ratings indicate default. The issuer has failed to meet one or more of its financial commitments and has entered into a formal wind-down process.

‘BBB’ ratings indicate that expectations of credit risk are currently low. The capacity for payment of financial commitments is considered adequate, but adverse business or economic conditions are more likely to impair this capacity.

‘A’ ratings denote expectations of low credit risk. The capacity for payment of financial commitments is considered strong. This capacity may, nevertheless, be more vulnerable to adverse business or economic conditions than higher ratings.

\'AAA\' ratings denote the lowest expectation of default risk. They\'re assigned only in cases of exceptionally strong capacity for payment of financial commitments. This capacity is highly unlikely to be adversely affected by foreseeable events.
‘B’ ratings indicate that material credit risk is present. Adverse business, financial, or economic conditions will likely impair capacity.
‘C’ indicates exceptionally high levels of credit risk. While payments may still be met, conditions point to a very high risk of missed payments in the near term.

\'RD\' ratings denote an issuer that has defaulted on one or more of its commitments, yet continues to meet others. It\'s a partial default state whereby the issuer hasn\'t entered into a formal wind-down process.

‘BB’ ratings indicate an elevated vulnerability to credit risk, particularly in the event of adverse changes in business or economic conditions over time. However, business or financial alternatives may be available to allow financial commitments to be met.

\'CCC\' ratings indicate substantial credit risk. Default is a real possibility. Capacities for meeting financial commitments are uncertain and reliant on favourable business, financial, and economic conditions.

‘AA’ ratings denote expectations of very low credit risk. They indicate a very strong capacity for payment of financial commitments. This capacity isn\'t significantly vulnerable to foreseeable events.
‘CC’ ratings indicate very high levels of credit risk. A default of some kind appears probable, and the bondholder\'s protections are minimal.
Very high levels of credit risk

A measure of how a bond’s duration changes as the interest rate changes. The higher the convexity, the more the bond price will increase when interest rates fall. It\'s used to measure exposure to interest rate risk.

The weighted average time it takes for a bond’s cash flows (interest and principal) to repay the initial investment, measured in years. It represents the \"balancing point\" of your investment. Generally, the higher it is, the more sensitive the bond\'s price will be to interest rate changes.

Measures the estimated percentage change in a bond’s price for every 1% change in interest rates. It’s a quick way to estimate your risk. For example, if a bond has a modified duration of 5 and rates rise 1%, your bond price may likely be expected to drop by about approximately 5%, while a 1% fall would most likely be expected to increase its price by about 5%.

Bankruptcy is a serious red flag for investors.

Recovery for shareholders is rare and highly uncertain.

Always monitor official announcements and seek professional advice if needed
Other important things to keep in mind regarding a bankruptcy

If you own shares, there is a high risk of losing most or all of your investment.

Shareholders are last in line to be paid after creditors, lenders, and bondholders.

The stock may continue trading, often at very low prices, but it may eventually be delisted or canceled.
What does this mean for you?
Bankruptcy is a legal process a company enters when it can’t pay its debts. It may try to restructure and continue operating (reorganization) or shut down and sell its assets (liquidation).

To restructure debts and try to survive financially 

To close down when recovery isn’t possible and distribute remaining assets 

Causes may include poor business performance, high debt, lawsuits, or economic downturns.

Important dates to keep in mind about a dividend:

Declaration Date
The date the company announces it will pay a dividend, including the amount, and payment date.

Ex-Dividend Date
To be eligible for the dividend, you must buy the shares before this date. Investors who purchase on or after this date will not receive the upcoming dividend.

Payment Date
The dividend is paid to eligible shareholders on this date—either as cash or additional shares, depending on the type of dividend.
What are the tax implications of cash dividends?

You get actual cash credited to your account — no need to sell your shares.

The stock price typically drops by the dividend amount on the ex-dividend date, as that value is paid out.

Your investment value doesn’t increase, but you receive part of it as cash in hand.

It’s like the company saying, “Here’s a portion of our earnings — thank you for being a shareholder.”
What does this mean for you?

A cash dividend is when a company shares its profits by paying cash directly to its shareholders.\nFor example, if a company declares a $1 dividend and you own 100 shares, you’ll receive $100 in cash.

To reward shareholders regularly — especially if they generate stable profits.

To signal financial strength and confidence in future cash flows. Many mature or stable companies (like utility firms or blue-chip stocks) pay regular dividends.

Cash dividends are often seen as a positive sign, especially for income-focused investors.

Other important things to keep in mind regarding a delisting:

Delisting can affect the liquidity and value of your shares.

Involuntary delistings (e.g., due to poor performance or non-compliance) may signal higher risk.

Always check official communication from the company or your broker for details and next steps.

If you own shares, you still hold ownership in the company.

However, after delisting, the shares may become harder to buy or sell, and may only trade over-the-counter (OTC) or not at all.

In some cases, especially in voluntary delistings, shareholders may receive a buyout offer from the company or acquirer.
What does this mean for you?
Delisting means a company\'s shares are removed from a stock exchange. After delisting, the shares are no longer available for trading on that exchange.

To go private and reduce regulatory costs or public scrutiny.

Due to a merger or acquisition.

Failure to meet listing requirements, like minimum share price or market value.
Why do companies do stock delisting?

Earnings calls can impact the stock price, especially if results or commentary are better or worse than expected.\n\nListening to or reading a summary of the call can give helpful insight into the company’s strategy and confidence level.
Other important things to keep in mind?

You can hear directly from company leaders about how the business is doing and what they expect going forward.

Management discusses key numbers like revenue, profit, and expenses, and may explain any major changes or challenges.

Investors and analysts often use this information to make more informed decisions.
What does this mean for you?
An earnings call is a live conference where a company’s management discusses its financial results for the quarter or year. It usually happens shortly after the company releases its earnings report.

To maintain transparency and keep investors informed.

To answer questions from analysts and explain the company’s performance in more detail.

It’s also a chance to share the company’s future plans or guidance.
Why do companies do earnings call?

For example, in a 2-for-1 forward split:

You get more shares. If you had 1 share previously, after the event you’ll have 2.

The price per share drops. If the old price was $1000, it becomes $500 after the split.

The total value of your investment stays the same.

You just own more shares, each worth less— so nothing changes in terms of how much your investment is worth (not counting normal market moves).
What does this mean for you?
A forward stock split is when a company increases the number of its shares by dividing each existing share into multiple new ones.\nFor example, in a 2-for-1 split, 1 share becomes 2 shares.
What is a forward stock split?

Generally, companies do it to make shares more affordable so more people can invest. It can increase trading activity because lower-priced shares attract more buyers.\n\nIt’s also often seen as a positive signal that the company is growing or doing well.

Stock-for-stock merger – You get shares in the new or acquiring company in exchange for your current shares.

Cash deal – You get a fixed cash amount per share; your shares are canceled.

Mixed deal – A combination of cash and shares.

Merger of equals – Two similar-sized companies combine to form a new company.

Multi-party mergers – More than two companies merge into a single entity, often for scale or efficiency.

Each type affects shareholders differently — but in all cases, the company will clearly explain the terms and next steps for investors.
What are different types of mergers?

If you own shares in a company that merges, your shares might get converted into new shares, shares of the other company, or be bought out for cash — depending on the merger terms.

Sometimes, you may end up holding shares in a larger, combined company.

Or, your shares may disappear and be replaced with a fixed cash payout.

The overall impact depends on the specific deal — but as a shareholder, you’re always notified in advance with full details.
What does this mean for you?

A merger is when two or more companies combine to become one.\nThis can happen in different ways — for example, two companies may merge and operate as a single new entity, or one company may fully absorb another.

To grow faster by combining resources, talent, or customer bases.

To expand into new markets or products.

To become more competitive or efficient by reducing duplication.

Mergers are usually seen as a strategic business move, though the actual impact on share price can vary.

In a 1-for-2 reverse split:

You’ll have fewer shares. If you had 2 shares before, now you’ll have 1.

The price per share goes up. If the old price was $500, it becomes $1,000 after the split.

The total value of your investment stays the same.
You just own fewer shares, each worth more — so nothing changes in terms of how much your investment is worth (not counting normal market moves).
What does this mean for you?

A reverse stock split is a corporate action in which a company reduces the number of its outstanding shares by consolidating multiple existing shares into a smaller number of shares.\nFor example, in a 1-for-2 reverse split, every 2 existing shares are combined into 1 new share
What is a reverse stock split?

To raise the share price — especially if it’s gotten very low.

To meet minimum price rules set by stock exchanges (like Nasdaq or NYSE).

To improve how the stock is perceived — since very low-priced stocks can seem risky to some investors.

A reverse stock split doesn’t change how the business is performing. But if a company does this often or in large amounts, it might be a sign that it’s facing challenges.

If you hold shares in the parent company at the time of the spinoff:

You’ll usually receive shares in the new company automatically, in proportion to your existing holdings.

Usually, your original shares remain unaffected — you’ll now hold shares in two separate companies.

Note: The total value of your holdings may initially remain similar, but the market value of each company’s shares may change over time based on performance
What does this mean for you?

A spinoff or demerger is when a company separates part of its business to form a new, independent company. A shareholder usually get shares in the new company, in addition to keeping their original shares.

To focus on core business areas by separating unrelated or lower-growth divisions.

To allow each company to operate independently, with its own management and strategy.

To potentially unlock greater shareholder value, as the market may better appreciate the individual businesses.
Why do companies undergo a spin off?

You’re not required to sell your shares — it’s optional.

After the buyback, there are fewer shares available in the market.

If you keep your shares, your ownership percentage in the company slightly increases.

This can potentially lead to higher earnings per share (EPS) and sometimes a higher stock price, though it’s not guaranteed.

You may also benefit indirectly if the buyback signals that the company is confident in its future.
What does this mean for you?

A stock buyback (also called a share repurchase) is when a company buys back its own shares from the open market or directly from shareholders.\nThese bought-back shares are usually canceled or held in the company’s treasury.

To return value to shareholders (similar to dividends).

To improve financial ratios like EPS by reducing the number of shares.

If the company believes its stock is undervalued and wants to invest in itself.

To offset dilution from employee stock option plans.

A buyback is generally seen as a positive signal, but its impact depends on how and why it’s done.
Why do companies do stock buyback?

Ex-Dividend Date

Payment Date
The dividend is paid to eligible shareholders on this date—either as cash or additional shares, depending on the type of dividend.
Important dates to keep in mind about a dividend

You receive more shares — no action needed on your part.

The price per share adjusts downward, so the total value of your investment stays the same (just like slicing a pie into more pieces).

Your ownership percentage in the company doesn't change — everyone gets extra shares proportionally.

You don’t receive any cash, but your number of shares increases.

It’s like getting bonus shares, but not extra money.
What does this mean for you?
A stock dividend is when a company gives additional shares to its shareholders.\nFor example, in a 10% stock dividend, you get 1 extra share for every 10 shares you already own.

To reward shareholders without spending cash.

To make the stock more affordable or liquid by increasing the number of shares.

Sometimes used by growing companies that want to reinvest profits but still offer something to shareholders.

Stock dividends are generally seen as a neutral or mildly positive sign, especially if the company has strong growth prospects.

You don’t need to do anything — the shares you own remain the same.

Only the symbol that appears in your portfolio or trading app changes.

The company’s ownership, share price, and your investment value are not affected.

It's just a label change, not a change in what you own.
What does this mean for you?
A symbol change is when a company updates the ticker symbol used to identify its stock on an exchange.\nFor example, if “ABCD” is the old symbol, it might change to “XYZ.”

After a merger or rebranding (e.g., Facebook changed its symbol from FB to META).

To better reflect a new name, business focus, or identity.

Sometimes after corporate restructuring like a spin-off or acquisition.

These changes are purely cosmetic and do not impact the stock’s value or your rights as a shareholder.

The government bonds and corporate bonds lists are grouped by issuer type - either governments (regional, national or supranational level) or corporations. They are provided for informational purposes only.

‘Highest Coupons’ list shows 20 bonds with the highest fixed coupon rates, ranked from the highest rate. The coupon rate is the fixed annual interest payment that the bond pays, expressed as a percentage of its face value. Please note that a bond’s coupon rate does not represent its total return or yield. Coupon payments are not guaranteed, and there is a risk that the issuer may not meet its payment obligations. This list is created by us on the basis of data from Fitch Inc. It is provided for informational purposes only and it is not an investment advice or a recommendation to buy, hold or sell any bond.

‘Highest Yielding’ list shows 20 bonds with the highest yield to maturity, ranked from the highest yield. The yield to maturity represents an estimated annual return an investor would earn if the bond is held until maturity, and provided that all coupon payments are made as scheduled and reinvested at the same rate, and that the principal is repaid in full at maturity. Some of these bonds may also be callable, meaning the issuer could redeem them before maturity, which may reduce the expected yield. This estimate may fluctuate over time and is not guaranteed, so actual returns may differ. Bonds with higher yields typically also carry higher risks, such as greater credit or market risk, including the risk of default of the issuer. This list is created by us on the basis of data from Fitch Inc. It is provided for informational purposes only and it is not an investment advice or a recommendation to buy, hold or sell any bond.

Index and non-equity ETF lists are grouped by the type of exposure they provide. Index ETFs track performance of entire or subset of market indices, and typically offer broader market exposure across markets and sectors. These lists are created by us and are provided for informational purposes only.

‘Maturing Soon’ list shows bonds that will mature within the next two years, ranking from soonest to latest maturity date. At maturity, the bond issuer repays the principal amount to investors, and interest payments stop. Some of these bonds may be callable, meaning the issuer could redeem them before the stated maturity date. Returns are not guaranteed, and there is a risk that the issuer may not meet its payment obligations. This list is created by us on the basis of data from Fitch Inc., and is provided for informational purposes only.

‘Most Shorted’ lists CFDs with the largest short interest. For short CFD positions on dividend-paying securities, dividends are also deducted from your available cash balance and should be considered in your risk management strategy. The list has been created by us on the basis of internal data. Spousal consent is a specific requirement set out in the Lithuanian Civil Code. As securities held with Revolut Securities Europe UAB are considered the joint property of you and your spouse, the law requires you to obtain his/her consent to make transactions in investment products.

If your spouse is not a Revolut customer, you can satisfy the spousal consent requirement by providing us with one of the following documents via the in-app chat:

  • A power of attorney issued by the \'Register of Powers of Attorney of State Enterprise Centre of Registers\'. Instructions to obtain and submit this to us can be found here; or
  • The notarised marriage agreement that determines the ownership rights of the spouses in financial instruments; or
  • A notarised power of attorney of your spouse authorising you to enter into transactions for financial instruments.

Please contact support via in-app chat when you have the documents you need.

The annual rate that accumulates while the note is live and is paid along with the face value upon a call event if the required conditions are met, expressed as a percentage of the note\'s face value.

The threshold the underlying assets\' performance must meet or exceed on an observation date for a call event to happen. It is expressed as a percentage of the assets\' initial level, which is fixed at product launch.
The initial date on which the underlying assets\' performance is checked against the call barrier to determine if the first call event happens.
Defines how often the conditions for a call event are checked on observation dates and, if met, the note is called.

Defines the performance used to check against call conditions, measured on an observation date. Lowest asset performance evaluates the worst-performing asset within a basket, while average asset performance uses the combined average return of a basket of assets. Single asset performance is applicable when the note has only one underlying asset.
The early maturity condition is checked against the performance of one underlying asset, measured at each observation date.
The early maturity condition is checked against the performance of one underlying asset, measured at each observation date.
The early maturity condition is checked against the performance of one underlying asset, measured at each observation date.
The amount paid if a call event occurs, ending the investment, expressed as a percentage of the note\'s face value.

The threshold the underlying assets\' performance must meet or exceed on the final observation date for the note to pay the face value in full at maturity. It is expressed as a percentage of the assets\' initial level, which is fixed at product launch.
The minimum amount that is paid on maturity regardless of the performance of the underlying assets, expressed as a percentage of the note\'s face value.

Defines the performance used to check against the capital barrier and determines the performance level used to calculate the amount paid at maturity. Lowest asset performance evaluates the worst-performing asset within a basket, while average asset performance uses the combined average return of a basket of assets. Single asset performance is applicable when the note has only one underlying asset.

The starting point for calculating any capital loss if the capital barrier is broken at the final observation date, expressed as a percentage of the assets\' initial level, which is fixed at product launch.

The threshold the underlying assets\' performance must meet or exceed on an observation date for a coupon to be paid. It is expressed as a percentage of the assets\' initial level, which is fixed at product launch.
The annual rate that determines the potential coupon payment amounts, expressed as a percentage of the note\'s face value.

Coupon type defines how coupon payments work. Guaranteed coupons are paid regardless of the underlying assets\' performance. For conditional coupons, a \"memory\" feature means missed coupons are deferred and might be paid later, while \"non-memory\" means missed coupons are not deferred for the future.
Coupon type defines how coupon payments work. A guaranteed coupon is determined upfront and paid regardless of the underlying asset\'s performance.
Coupon type defines how coupon payments work. A guaranteed coupon is determined upfront and paid regardless of the underlying asset\'s performance.
Coupon type defines how coupon payments work. A guaranteed coupon is determined upfront and paid regardless of the underlying asset\'s performance.
The initial date on which the underlying assets\' performance is checked against the coupon barrier to determine if the first coupon payment is due.
Defines how often the conditions for a coupon payment are checked on observation dates and, if met, paid.

Defines the performance used to check against coupon conditions, measured on an observation date. Lowest asset performance evaluates the worst-performing asset within a basket, while average asset performance uses the combined average return of a basket of assets. Single asset performance is applicable when the note has only one underlying asset.
The note\'s return is linked to the performance of one underlying asset, measured at each observation date.

The note\'s return is linked to the performance of one underlying asset, measured at each observation date.
The rate by which the capital loss increases for every 1%% the underlying assets fall below the strike, expressed as a multiple.
The maximum return that the note will pay, even if the underlying assets grow significantly above the strike, expressed as a percentage of the note\'s face value.

Defines the performance level used to calculate the return or loss, measured on the final observation date. Lowest asset performance evaluates the worst-performing asset within a basket, while average asset performance uses the combined average return of a basket of assets. Single asset performance is applicable when the note has only one underlying asset.
The rate by which the return increases for every 1%% the underlying assets gain above the strike, expressed as a multiple.

The starting point for calculating any return or capital loss based on the performance of the underlying assets, expressed as a percentage of the assets\' initial level, which is fixed at product launch.
The total scheduled lifespan of the structured note from its issue date to the maturity date.
The nominal or principal amount of a security used as the baseline to calculate potential returns, coupons, and repayment at maturity.
The International Securities Identification Number (ISIN) is a globally recognized, unique 12-character code used to identify a specific financial security.
The price at which a structured note is initially offered and sold to investors, representing the actual initial cost of the investment.
The date the final level of the underlying asset(s) is recorded to determine the final payout, provided the note has not been called earlier.
The date on which the structured note is issued as a new security.
The scheduled end date of the investment when the final calculated amount is repaid, provided the note has not been called earlier.
The execution date of the transaction, marking the economic start of the investment and establishing the baseline prices for the underlying assets.

The Service fee includes our fee and the Fund service fee which is paid to the Fund manager. It is an ongoing charge calculated as a percentage of the value of the shares you hold in the money market fund. The service fee is calculated daily and is automatically deducted from the daily return you receive.

Investing in money market funds is an alternative to depositing money in traditional savings accounts offered by banks. Money market funds typically offer higher return rates in environments of high central bank interest rates, but the fund's returns are not guaranteed and can move in an unfavourable direction in adverse market conditions. It is offered in collaboration with Fidelity International, one of the largest asset managers in the world.

This money market fund is a sub-fund of Fidelity Institutional Liquidity Fund plc, authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland. You invest in share class R Flex Distributing shares. 

The Fund Manager is FIL Investment Management (Luxembourg) S.A., Ireland Branch, a company regulated by Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier in Luxembourg and authorised to act as a management company to UCITS (address: 2a, Rue Albert Borschette, BP 2174, L-1021 Luxembourg). The Fund has delegated its day-to-day management to the Fund Manager, a wholly owned subsidiary of Fidelity International.

For more information, read the KID and the Prospectus under regulatory documents.
Money saved in a bank and generating interest for a fixed time period; includes time deposits, certificates of deposit, shares in other money market funds and cash.

Top-grade debt issued by governments, financial institutions and corporates that borrow money to pay for some of their expenses; includes government and corporate bonds, bank obligations, commercial paper and asset backed commercial paper, repurchase agreements (repos) and reverse repos.

Annual Percentage Yield (APY) represents the final return you get from your money. The return rates are variable and have a similar behaviour as central bank interest rates of the concerned currency given the underlying investments of the fund. The return rates are calculated every day by the fund and made available to you through the app net of fees, which means you'll always have the most up-to-date rates available.

Your returns are compounded monthly but paid daily. This means that the return earned during the month is reinvested at the beginning of the month (if not withdrawn). However, we will pay you interest on the capital that you have on a daily basis.

When you add money, you'll receive a return on your investment when the APY is positive and if the return accumulated balance is high enough (above 1 cent). Here’s an example:

We've carefully selected this fund for it's stability and low-risk. It also has one of the highest possible ratings from credit agencies.

A money market fund is a Packaged Retail Investment Product (PRIP). This means the money you'll receive back from your investment will vary depending on the performance of the underlying investments of the fund, which are not directly purchased by you. This PRIP is authorised in Ireland and its Key Information Document supervised by the Central Bank of Ireland.

Thanks to the underlying short-term and high-quality investments of the fund, this fund is overall low risk: it has the minimum risk indicator of 1/7.
The fund has the highest rating from independent credit rating agencies and means the underlying assets of this fund have high levels of capital security and low levels of interest rate sensitivity.

The risk indicator compares this investment's risk against other products. It shows how likely it is that the fund will lose money because of market movements or if FIL Investment Management (Luxembourg) S.A isn't able to pay you. 

This fund rates its risk using PRIIPs Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014. This rates the potential losses from future performance at a low level. Poor market conditions are also unlikely to impact the ability to pay you. Returns may increase or decrease due to currency fluctuations – this isn't reflected in the risk level.

This fund doesn't include any protection from future market performance, so you could lose some or all of your investment.

If FIL Investment Management (Luxembourg) S.A. isn't able to pay you what's owed, you could lose your entire investment.

◦ Every time you pay with your joint card, we round up your purchase to the nearest $1,000 and automatically save the difference in this Pocket.

• What is the multiplier?
◦ The multiplier lets you save more with every purchase.
◦ For example, if your spare change is $400 and you choose a x2 multiplier, we’ll save $800 in your Pocket.

◦ If you spend $1,600, we save $400 in your Pocket to round your purchase up to the next $1,000.

Assets under management (AuM) is the total market value of the investments that a person or entity handles on behalf of investors. AuM fluctuates daily, depending on the flow of investors\' money in and out of the fund, the performance of the underlying assets and reinvested dividends (if applicable).

The rate of return based on the most recent income dividend. The yield is calculated as the most recent monthly dividend distribution multiplied by 12 (or 4 if the fund distributes dividends quarterly) and divided by the latest NAV or market price.

The rate of return based on the most recent income dividend. The yield is calculated as the most recent monthly dividend distribution multiplied by 12 (or 4 if the fund distributes dividends quarterly) and divided by the latest Net Asset Value (NAV) or market price.

Interests, dividends, and other sources of income earned by the ETF\'s underlying assets that are proportionally distributed to the investors. The indicated amount represents the most recent dividends paid out on per-share basis. The income dividend is paid out periodically and may vary depending on the assets held by ETF.

The Net Asset Value (NAV) of an ETF is calculated by taking the most recent closing price of all securities held by the ETF (such as shares, bonds and cash) subtracting any liabilities (such as Total Expense Ratio), and dividing that figure by the number of shares outstanding. NAV is most often expressed as the value per share.
Gross total expense ratio as listed in the Fee & Expense table in the prospectus.

Prospectus Gross Management Fee Ratio – An expense ratio reported in the Fee & Expense Table in the prospectus representing the investment advisory fee management fee and administrative fees payable to the investment advisor or its affiliate and that are not included in the Prospectus Gross Other Expense Ratio.
A proportion of generated income distributed to investors. Collected on a per share basis.
Latest Price NAV provides the most recent NAV Lipper has available for the asset.
Net total expense ratio as listed in the Fee & Expense table in the prospectus.

An expense ratio calculated by subtracting any Prospectus Fee Waiver related to the advisor from the Prospectus Gross Management Fee Ratio. It represents the net (after waiver) investment advisory fee management fee and administrative fees payable to the investment advisor or its affiliate and that are not included in the Prospectus Gross Other Expense Ratio.
The Total Net Assets (TNA) of the fund. TNA represents the total funds under management for net of fees and expenses for a particular date.

The total expense ratio (TER) is a measure of the total cost of a fund to an investor. Costs are deducted from assets and are reflected in the price of the ETF. The TER, calculated by dividing the total annual cost by the fund\'s total assets averaged over that year, is presented as a percentage.

The summary risk indicator is a guide to the level of risk of this product compared to other products. It shows how likely it is that the product will lose money because of movements in the markets or because the product manufacturer is not able to pay you.\nBefore you invest, carefully evaluate the SRI and the rest of information within the Key Information Document (KID)

The SRRI is designed to provide a consistent calculation and presentation of the risk of UCITS funds. The rating is based on the volatility of the fund over the past 5 years. The SRRI is a numerical scale between 1 (low risk/volatility) and 7 (high risk/volatility).\nBefore you invest, carefully evaluate the SRRI and the rest of information within the Key Investor Information Document (KIID)

Accrued interest is the amount of interest earned on a bond, but not yet collected. When you buy a bond, you pay that amount up front so you can receive the full coupon next time it’s due.
The clean price is the price of a bond not including accrued interest payments. Bond prices are displayed in terms of the clean price on price charts.
The price displayed is how much it would cost to buy the minimum denomination of this bond at the current indicative market price. This price represents the dirty ask price.
A dirty price refers to the cost of a bond that includes accrued interest. This is the price at which you would buy or sell the bond in the market.

A bond\'s face value is the amount the issuer provides to the bondholder, once maturity is reached. Bond prices are quoted in terms of percentage of face value e.g. a price of 99 for a bond with a face value of $100 means that one bond is valued at $99.
This is the minimum increment sensitivity in currency value that the broker will accept for this bond.
The lot price is equivalent to the minimum currency value that you can trade of a bond. It is calculated by multiplying the dirty price by the number of units in the lot.
Units represent how many underlying minimum bond denominations are in a lot. It is calculated by dividing the minimum investment increment by the face value of the bond.

Long-Term Asset Funds (LTAFs) can invest into fixed assets, infrastructure, or complex financial products, all of which are relatively hard to sell. Investors who do not remain invested for the long-term may not get back all of their money. It may take many years to make a profit on the investment.

You should carry out your own research, so that you understand what you are investing in.
You should be ready to invest for the long term and, during this time, the value of your investment may go up or down. You may lose money on your investment.

This LTAF accepts requests to sell units only once a month and there is also a 90-day waiting period before the value of your units is determined and you receive your money. This means that:

If you choose to sell your units on 2 January, and the trading day is the 15th of the month, you won’t get any money back until approximately 20 April, assuming a few extra days for the trade to close and funds to transfer.

The value of the units you sell will be at the price set on 15 April if it is a business day, or else the next business day after it.

Once your redemption request has been approved, you cannot cancel your request.

Once you have submitted your request to close your Revolut Wealth Inc. account (also referred to as “investment account”), you will no longer be able to access your account or the data associated with it via the Revolut App. This includes trade confirmations, tax documents and/or statements you may have received as a Wealth client. Tax documents, statements and confirmations will still be available from the custodian’s website.

Once you have submitted your request to close your Robo-Advisor Account with us, you will no longer be able to access your Account or view or download associated documents you’ve received as our client, except for Portfolio account statement which will be available to download via the App for 6 months after your Account closure.

Initiation of Account Closure: Once you have submitted your request to close your Robo-Advisor Account with us, you will no longer be able to access your Robo-Advisor Account, and view or download associated documents you’ve received as our client. If you need access to your account statements after your Robo-Advisor Account has been closed, please contact our chat support team for assistance.
Termination of Services: Upon account closure, all services associated with your account will be terminated, including any recurring investments and/or withdrawals.

Once you have submitted your request to close your investment account no further portfolio rebalancing or portfolio changes will occur. Any open pending orders will be canceled on a best effort’s basis. If a pending order is filled before it can be canceled, it will be treated as an open securities position.

Once you have submitted your request to close your Robo-Advisor Account no further Portfolio rebalancing or Portfolio changes will occur. Any open pending orders will be canceled on a best effort’s basis. If a pending order is filled before it can be canceled, it will be treated as an open securities position and closed accordingly.

Processing of account closure request: Once you have submitted your request to close your Robo-Advisor Account, we will proceed to liquidate your existing portfolio holdings. No further portfolio rebalancing or “edit portfolio” will occur. (“Edit portfolio” refers to the change of portfolio from one risk level to another). We will attempt to cancel any open pending orders on a best-effort basis, but please be aware that cancellation is not guaranteed. If an open pending order is filled before it can be cancelled, it will be treated as an open position.
Monthly Investment management fees will be pro-rated to the date of the account closure, and deducted accordingly.

Any open positions in your Robo-Advisor Account will be liquidated by placing a sell order for the full number of shares of each financial instrument in your Portfolio. During this time and at order execution, the value of your investment may fall as well as rise and you may get back less than your initial investment, and in some cases, you may lose your entire initial investment. Closure of your Account may have adverse effects on your investment objectives.

Any open positions in your Robo-Advisor Account will be liquidated by placing a sell order for the full number of shares of each financial instrument in your Portfolio. During this time and at order execution, the value of your investment may fall or rise, and you may get back less than your initial investment, and in some cases you may lose your entire initial investment.

Any open securities positions in your investment account will be sold. During this time and at order execution, the value of your investment may fall as well as rise and you may get back less than your initial investment, and in some cases, you may lose your entire initial investment.

Any cash balance, including sale proceeds, in your Account will be transferred to your Revolut current account. In the majority of cases it will take up to 5 business days for us to process your request to close your Robo-Advisor Account and transfer the funds to your Revolut current account. We will not be able to transfer cash balance to you unless all remaining trades have settled. Your Account will be deemed closed when there is a EUR 0,00 trading balance.
Any cash balances (including sale proceeds) in your Robo-Advisor Account will be transferred to the Revolut Retail Account you hold with Revolut Technologies Singapore Pte Ltd.
Any cash balance in your Revolut Wealth Inc. Pocket will be withdrawn to your Retail Pocket.

Monthly Management fees will be charged proportionally to the days you’ve used the Services during the billing period and will be deducted from the proceeds of sale of the financial instruments in your Portfolio. Upon the completion of Account closure, no further Portfolio management Services will be provided to you.

Processing Time: Account closure requests will typically be processed within five (5) business days. However, this timeline may be extended due to pending transactions, corporate actions, or other factors outside Our control. We will not be able to transfer the funds to you unless all remaining trades have settled. Your Robo Advisor Account will be deemed closed when all cash is transferred out of your Robo-Advisor account.
In the majority of cases it will take up to 3-5 business days for us to process your request to close your investment account and the proceeds from the sale of each security to settle.

Outstanding Fees: Any outstanding fees or charges you owe to Us will be deducted from your account balance prior to being transferred back to your Revolut Retail Account. If there are any outstanding fees or charges which are not covered by the account balance, We reserve the right to claim back the fees owed for the services by debiting the same from your Revolut Retail Account.

Once your investment account is closed and all trades have settled, you can withdraw cash from your USD Retail Pocket. “Unsettled sale proceeds” are not available to withdraw until all remaining trades have settled. Your investment account will be deemed closed when there is a $0 trading balance.

Tax Implications: You are solely responsible for any tax liabilities arising from the closure of your account. We do not provide tax advice and recommend that you consult with a tax professional regarding potential tax implications.
Upon the completion of account closure, no further investment management services or advice will be provided.

Data Retention: We will retain certain account and personal information as required by applicable laws and regulations, even after your account has been closed. This data will be protected in accordance with our privacy policy.

Reactivation: Once your Account is closed, it cannot be reopened. Should you wish to re-engage our Robo-advisor services, you will be required to create a new account. For the avoidance of doubt, the new account will not reflect prior transactions from the closed accounts.

A cashflow statement shows the company\'s cash movements during a particular period

This is defined as Shareholder\'s Equity divided by the Shares Outstanding at the end of the most recent fiscal year.

This is Cash Flow for the most recent fiscal year divided by the Average Shares Outstanding for the same period. Cash Flow is defined as the sum of Income After Taxes minus Preferred Dividends and General Partner Distributions plus Depreciation, Depletion and Amortisation.

This is the Total Cash plus Short Term Investments divided by the Shares Outstanding at the end of the most recent fiscal year. NOTE: This does NOT include cash equivalents that may be reported under long term assets.
This is the Adjusted Income Available to Common Stockholders for the trailing twelve months divided by the trailing twelve month Diluted Weighted Average Shares Outstanding.
This value is the Total Revenue for the most recent fiscal year divided by the Average Diluted Shares Outstanding for the same period.
This value is the current percentage dividend yield based on the present cash dividend rate. It is calculated as the Indicated Annual Dividend divided by the current Price, multiplied by 100.
This ratio is the percentage of the Primary/Basic Earnings Per Share Excluding Extraordinary Items paid to common stockholders in the form of cash dividends during the most recent fiscal year.
This is the Dividend Per Share amount paid by the company for the most recent fiscal year.

This is the number of freely traded shares in the hands of the public. Float is calculated as Shares Outstanding minus Shares Owned by Insiders, 5% Owners, and Rule 144 Shares. NOTE: For the first year after an initial public offering (IPO) the float will be the number of shares issued in the IPO.
This value is calculated by multiplying the current Price by the current number of Shares Outstanding.
Represents the number of common shares outstanding in a company.

Beta is a measure of a company\'s common stock price volatility relative to the market. Beta is the slope of the 60 month regression line of the percentage price change of the stock relative to the percentage price change of the local index. Beta values are not calculated if less than 40 months of pricing is available.
The low and high price of a security within one day\'s trading session.
The low and high price of a security within a 52-week period.
The low and high price of a security within a 5-year period.
The price at which a security first trades upon the opening of an exchange each trading day.
This is the 3 month average daily volume calculated as the total volume divided by the number of trading days in the last 3 months.
Number of shares traded of the stock on the current day, or previous trading day when the market is currently closed.

This value is calculated as the Income After Taxes for the most recent fiscal year divided by the Average Total Assets, expressed as a percentage. Average Total Assets is the average of the Total Assets at the beginning and the end of the year.

This value is calculated as the Income Available to Common Stockholders for the most recent fiscal year divided by the Average Common Equity and is expressed as a percentage. Average Common Equity is the average of the Common Equity at the beginning and the end of the year.
This value is the annual Income After Taxes divided by the average Total Long Term Debt, Other Long Term Liabilities, and Shareholders Equity, expressed as a percentage.

This value measures the percent of revenue left after paying all direct production expenses. It is calculated as annual Total Revenue minus annual Cost of Goods Sold divided by annual Total Revenue and multiplied by 100. NOTE: This item is only available for Industrial and Utility companies.
Also known as Return on Sales, this value is the Income After Taxes for the most recent fiscal year divided by Total Revenue for the same period and is expressed as a percentage.

This value measures the percent of revenues remaining after paying all operating expenses. It is calculated as annual Operating Income divided by annual Total Revenue, multiplied by 100. Operating Income is defined as Total Revenue minus Total Operating Expenses.
This is the Current Price divided by the latest annual Book Value Per Share.

This is the current Price divided by the annual Free Cash Flow Per Share. Free Cash Flow is calculated from the Statement of Cash Flows as Cash From Operations minus Capital Expenditures and Dividends Paid.

This ratio is calculated by dividing the current Price by the sum of the Diluted Earnings Per Share from continuing operations BEFORE Extraordinary Items and Accounting Changes for the latest annual period.
This is the current Price divided by the Sales Per Share for the most recent fiscal year.
All ratios are calculated for the latest fiscal year end, unless specified otherwise

Let us know why you want to close your Strategies account, or what we can improve

Once you have submitted your request to close your managed account, you will no longer be able to access your managed account or view or download associated documents, except for the managed account statements which will be available for download via the Revolut app for 6 months after your managed account closure. After this period, you may request a copy of your account statements by contacting us, and we will retain the underlying records for as long as required by applicable law.

Once you have submitted your request to close your managed account, we will stop managing your portfolio and no further portfolio rebalancing activities or changes to the portfolio will occur. We will use reasonable efforts to cancel any pending orders. If a pending order is filled before it can be canceled, it will be treated as an open position and will be closed in accordance with the Terms and Conditions.

Any open positions in your managed account will be liquidated by placing a sell order for all instruments held in your portfolio. Selling the instruments in your managed account may have tax consequences; we do not provide tax advice. The value of your investments may fall as well as rise and you may get back less than your initial investment, and in some cases, you may lose your entire initial investment. Closure of your managed account may have adverse effects on your investment objectives.

Any cash balance, including sale proceeds, in your managed account will be transferred to your Revolut current account. In the majority of cases it will take up to 5 business days for us to process your request to close your managed account and transfer the funds to your Revolut current account. We will not be able to transfer the cash balance to you unless all remaining transactions have settled and any amounts due to us have been paid. Your managed account will be closed when there are no open positions in your managed account and the cash balance is GBP 0,00 balance.

Monthly management fee will be charged for the managed portfolio services until your managed account is closed. The management fee accrues daily and and will be charged in proportion to the number of days in the billing period during which your managed account was active, up to and including the date your managed account is closed. The management fee will be deducted from the cash balance in your managed account (including any proceeds of sale of the instruments in your portfolio); where there is insufficient cash to cover it, we may recover any outstanding amount in accordance with the Terms of Business. Upon the completion of your managed account closure, no further managed portfolio services (including any advisory services provided as part of the managed portfolio services) will be provided to you.

You can set up Take profit and Stop loss to manage risks when investing. A Stop Loss becomes a market order when the set price is reached, so it may not fill at that exact stop price. When one of them gets triggered, the other one is automatically cancelled.

The Morningstar Fair Value Estimate guides investors to the long-term, intrinsic value of a stock, helping them see beyond the present market price.

Morningstar calculates the fair value estimate of a company based on a projection of how much cash the company will generate in the future. Morningstar analysts create custom industry and company assumptions to feed income statement, balance sheet, and capital investment assumptions into a proprietary discounted cash flow modeling template. Scenario analysis, in-depth competitive advantage analysis, and a variety of other analytical tools are used to augment the discounted cash flow process. The analyst discounts future cash flows using the weighted average of the costs of equity, debt, and preferred stock (and any other funding sources), using expected future proportionate long-term, market-value weights.

The Morningstar Fair Value Estimate is a projection/opinion and not a statement of fact. If Morningstar's base-case assumptions are true the market price will converge on Morningstar's fair value estimate over time, generally within three years. Investments in securities are subject to market and other risks. Past performance of a security may or may not be sustained in the future and is no indication of future performance.

Estimates both time- and money-weighted returns by assigning more weight to earlier cashflows, impacting the overall performance calculation.

Money weighted return (also known as Modified Dietz method) calculates portfolio performance by including the effects of top ups and withdrawals during the selected period. It is a useful measure for portfolio performance with more regular cashflows.
Estimates return on investment. Calculated as total profit-and-loss divided by a sum of buy amounts in the selected period.

Simple return calculates how much the value of your portfolio has increased/decreased over a given period of time, including any dividends received during the period. It does not account for the impact of time, top-ups or withdrawals. This method is commonly used for evaluating portfolio performance over a short period of time.
Measures returns while removing the impact of cashflows. It is a valid method for benchmarking and comparing performance across different portfolios.

Time-weighted return calculates portfolio performance by excluding the effects of top ups and withdrawals during the selected period. It is calculated by linking returns of shorter time periods while removing the effects of cashflows. This method is commonly used to compare performance across benchmarks or other portfolios.
